The One Thing Both Meanings Share

Even though the two meanings feel different on the surface, they share the same deep logic:

Something is taken, claimed, or assigned — and it now "belongs" to a specific person, group, or purpose.

In Meaning 1, the claiming is often informal and questionable. In Meaning 2, the claiming is formal and authorized. But in both cases, something is being pulled toward a particular owner or use.

Once you understand "appropriate," the word misappropriate becomes easy. It simply means to appropriate wrongly — especially to take money or resources that were meant for one purpose and use them for something else, usually dishonestly.

  • A charity treasurer uses donation money to pay for personal vacations. → She misappropriated the charity's funds.
Cultural Appropriation — A Phrase Worth Knowing

You will very often hear the phrase "cultural appropriation" in modern discussions. This is built directly on Meaning 1 of the verb. It refers to when people from one culture take elements — music, clothing, language, traditions, spiritual practices — from another culture (often a minority or historically oppressed one) and use them without proper understanding, respect, or credit.

For example, if someone from outside a particular indigenous community begins selling that community's sacred symbols as fashion accessories for profit, that is widely described as cultural appropriation. The elements of that culture have been appropriated — taken and used by those who don't belong to it.
How to Spot the Verb in a Sentence

Since "appropriate" looks identical as both a verb and an adjective, here's a simple trick:

  • If the word is followed by a noun (a thing being taken), it's the verb. → "She appropriated the funds."
  • If the word describes whether something fits or is suitable, it's the adjective. → "That was an appropriate response."

To appropriate something (verb) means:

  1. To take it and claim it as your own — often when you don't fully have the right to, whether that's someone's idea, land, culture, or creative work.
  2. To formally set it aside for a specific purpose — especially money or resources, in official or government settings.

The heart of the word is always the same: something is being claimed. The tone — whether questionable or perfectly legitimate — depends entirely on the situation.
945:
"Appropriately" means in a way that fits the situation perfectly — in a manner that is right, suitable, and correct for the specific circumstances at hand.

Think of it this way: every situation in life has invisible rules or expectations about how things should be done. When someone acts in a way that matches those expectations, they act appropriately. When they don't, they act inappropriately.

The word answers the question: "Was it done in the right way for this situation?"
The Key Insight: Context Is Everything

What makes this word so interesting is that what counts as "appropriate" shifts completely depending on the situation. There is no single standard. The rightness or suitability is always measured against the specific context.

For example:

  • Wearing a swimsuit is appropriately dressed at the beach. The same swimsuit at a funeral is not appropriately dressed — it's inappropriate.
  • Laughing loudly is appropriately expressive at a comedy show. At a library, it's not.
  • Speaking softly is appropriately quiet in a hospital. At a cricket match, you'd barely be heard.

The action itself (wearing clothes, laughing, speaking) isn't good or bad on its own. The word "appropriately" tells you that the manner of doing it matched what the situation called for.
What Kind of Word It Is, and How It Works

"Appropriately" is an adverb, which means it describes how something is done. It modifies verbs, adjectives, and other adverbs.

  • She dressed appropriately for the interview. (modifies a verb — describes how she dressed)
  • He responded appropriately to the criticism. (describes how he responded)
  • The punishment was appropriately severe. (modifies an adjective — tells you the severity was just right)
  • She spoke quite appropriately for the occasion. (modifies another adverb)
The Full Range of What It Can Mean

Because "appropriate" covers suitability across many dimensions, "appropriately" can refer to:

Behaviour and conduct:

The students behaved appropriately during the ceremony.

This means they acted in the way expected of students in that setting — quietly, respectfully, attentively.

Tone and language:

She spoke to her boss appropriately.

She used respectful, professional language — not too casual, not rude, not overly formal either.

Timing:

He arrived appropriately early for his job interview.

Not so early it was awkward, not late — just the right amount of early.

Amount or degree:

The charity was appropriately funded for the size of the project.

The money given matched what the project actually needed — not too little, not wastefully excessive.

Reaction or response:

She appropriately expressed concern when she heard the bad news.

Her emotional response fit the gravity of the situation. She didn't laugh, she didn't overreact — she responded in the way any thoughtful person would.
The Idea of an Invisible Standard

When someone says something was done "appropriately," they are measuring the action against some standard or expectation — a benchmark of what should happen in that situation.

This standard can come from:

  • Social norms (how people generally expect others to behave in a given setting)
  • Professional rules (how a doctor, teacher, or lawyer is expected to act)
  • Moral expectations (what a fair, honest, or kind person would do)
  • Practical requirements (what the task actually requires to succeed)

The engineer appropriately tested the bridge before opening it to the public.

Here, the standard is practical and safety-based. Testing before opening is what the situation demanded. Doing it was appropriate; skipping it would have been inappropriate and dangerous.

Like most adverbs, "appropriately" can be strengthened or softened:

  • Quite appropriately — clearly suitable, with some emphasis
  • Very appropriately — strongly fitting, especially noteworthy
  • Appropriately enough — used when the fitting nature of something is slightly ironic or unsurprising: "Appropriately enough, the award for best environmentalist was made from recycled materials."
  • Not entirely appropriately — a soft, polite way of saying something was a little off

Understanding "appropriately" becomes crystal clear when you look at its opposite. "Inappropriately" means doing something in a way that does not fit the situation — it's wrong, unsuitable, or out of place.

  • He inappropriately made jokes during the memorial service.
  • She inappropriately wore a party dress to a job interview at a law firm.
  • The teacher inappropriately shared a student's private information with other students.

Every time you see "inappropriately," the message is: this did not match what the situation called for, and usually there's a sense that the person should have known better.

One important nuance: who gets to decide what's "appropriate"? The answer is that it depends on the context. Sometimes society broadly agrees (shouting at a newborn baby's crib is inappropriate — nearly everyone would agree). But sometimes it's debatable.

Was his response to the criticism appropriately direct, or was it rude?

One person may say it was appropriately direct and honest. Another may say it crossed a line into rudeness. This is why you'll sometimes hear people argue over whether something was appropriate — because appropriateness is measured against standards, and people don't always share the same standards.

This doesn't mean the word is vague. It just means the word honestly reflects the way human judgement works.
How It Feels in a Sentence

"Appropriately" carries a quiet sense of approval and rightness. When you use it, you are not just describing what happened — you are gently confirming that it should have happened that way. There is a small note of satisfaction or validation in the word.

The firefighter appropriately prioritised rescuing the trapped child first.

The word "appropriately" here does more than describe the order of rescue. It signals: yes, that was the right call. That's how it should be done.

Compare to just saying "The firefighter rescued the trapped child first." That's a neutral fact. Adding "appropriately" is a quiet verdict: that was correct and fitting.

What it meansIn a way that fits, suits, or is right for the situation
What it depends onThe context — the situation, the setting, the expectations
What it signalsA quiet approval that the manner matched what was needed
Its oppositeInappropriately (done in a way that doesn't fit)
Its root adjectiveAppropriate (fitting, suitable, right for the context)

(Apologies — a small reference summary slipped in. The core explanations above are the substance.)

That is the complete picture of "appropriately." Its power lies in the idea that rightness is always relative to context — and this word is the elegant way English says "yes, it matched."
946:
Appropriation means the act of taking something and making it your own — setting it aside for a particular person, group, or purpose. The key idea baked into the word is that something is being claimed, allocated, or taken — sometimes with full authority to do so, and sometimes without.

Because this word lives in several different worlds (law, government, culture, and art), it can feel slippery. But once you understand its core engine — something being taken or set aside for a specific use — each meaning will click into place naturally.

1. The Everyday, General Meaning

In its most basic sense, appropriation is the act of taking something for your own use, often without asking permission. The thing being taken doesn't have to be a physical object — it can be an idea, a phrase, a style, or credit for someone else's work.

His appropriation of his colleague's research, without giving her any credit, was considered deeply unethical.

Here, he took something that wasn't his — not physically, but intellectually — and claimed it as his own. That act of taking-and-claiming is the appropriation.

Notice that this sense carries a negative tone. When used this way, it implies the taking was wrong, unfair, or at least questionable.

2. The Government and Financial Meaning

This is probably the most "official" and neutral use of the word, and you'll see it often in news about budgets and governments.

In this context, appropriation means the formal, official act of setting money aside for a specific purpose. A government body (like a parliament or congress) "appropriates" funds — meaning it officially decides that a specific amount of money will go toward a specific use and no other.

The government's appropriation of $2 billion for flood relief ensured the money could only be spent on that disaster and nothing else.

This meaning is almost always neutral or positive in tone. It simply describes a formal, legitimate process. The money isn't stolen — it's officially designated.

A helpful image: think of it like labelling a jar. The act of appropriation is the moment someone writes "FLOOD RELIEF" on the jar and puts the money inside. That money now belongs to that purpose.

3. Cultural Appropriation

This is the use you'll most commonly encounter in social and political conversations today, and it is always loaded with serious weight.

Cultural appropriation refers to when a person or group adopts specific elements from a culture that is not their own — its music, fashion, hairstyles, spiritual practices, language, food, or art forms — especially when they do so without proper understanding, respect, or acknowledgment, and often while the people of that original culture are discriminated against or disadvantaged.

The reason this causes controversy is the power imbalance at its core. It tends to happen when a more dominant or privileged group takes from a historically marginalized or oppressed group. The group doing the taking often receives praise, profit, or recognition for something that members of the original culture were (or still are) mocked, penalized, or excluded for.

Wearing a sacred ceremonial headdress as a Halloween costume is widely considered cultural appropriation.

Some critics accused the fashion brand of cultural appropriation for selling expensive versions of traditional handwoven textiles from an indigenous community, without crediting or compensating those artisans.

Why does it matter? Because the original culture often gets nothing — no credit, no money, no respect — while someone from outside takes the thing and profits from it or turns it into a trend. Meanwhile, the people from that culture may still face prejudice for the same things being celebrated when an outsider does them. That gap — between how the original culture is treated versus how the borrower is treated — is what makes this form of appropriation harmful in most people's eyes.

It's worth noting: not everyone agrees on exactly where the line is, and the debate around cultural appropriation is genuinely complex. Some argue that all cultures have always borrowed from each other, and that sharing is natural and even good. Others argue that context, power, and respect are what separate harmful appropriation from respectful cultural exchange. Both sides of this debate use the word "appropriation" — one to criticize it, and the other sometimes to challenge whether a particular act really qualifies.

4. Appropriation in Art

In the art world, appropriation has a specific technical meaning: the deliberate use of existing images, objects, or artworks within a new work of art, usually with the intention of commenting on, questioning, or transforming the meaning of the original.

This is largely a neutral to positive term in artistic circles. Famous artists have built entire careers around it.

Andy Warhol's paintings of Campbell's soup cans are a classic example of artistic appropriation — he took a mass-produced commercial image and placed it in a fine art context, asking the viewer to think differently about both.

The point of artistic appropriation is usually intellectual: the artist is making a statement about the original image or object by lifting it out of its original context and placing it somewhere new. It's intentional, creative, and often provocative.
Tone: When Is It Negative, Neutral, or Positive?

The same word carries very different emotional weight depending on context:

ContextTone
Taking someone's work or ideas without permissionNegative
Government allocating fundsNeutral / Positive
Taking from another culture without respectNegative / Contested
Using existing art to create new meaningNeutral / Positive
The Thread That Connects All Meanings

Even though appropriation appears in such different conversations, all its meanings share one DNA:

Something is being taken or claimed — and the question is always whether that taking is legitimate, respectful, and fair.

When the answer is yes (as in a government budget), the word is neutral. When the answer is no — or at least questionable — the word becomes a word of criticism and moral weight.

Once you internalize that core tension, you'll never be confused by appropriation again, no matter where you encounter it.
947:
Approval means a positive response toward something or someone — a signal that says "yes, this is good" or "yes, you may go ahead." It captures the idea of finding something acceptable, correct, or pleasing, whether that comes from a feeling inside you or from an official decision by an authority.

The word works in two main directions: one is emotional (how you feel about something), and the other is official/formal (a decision made by a person or organization in power). Both share the same core: something has been judged and found to be okay, right, or good.

1. An Expression or Feeling That Something Is Good

This is the personal, emotional sense. When you look at something and feel that it is right, pleasing, or satisfactory — and you show that feeling — you are expressing approval.

This kind of approval doesn't require any formal process. It can be a smile, a nod, a word of praise, or simply a positive attitude toward something.

Examples:

  • She looked at her son's drawing and smiled in approval.
  • He glanced at the new employee's work with quiet approval.
  • The crowd cheered in approval when the singer walked on stage.
  • The teacher's nod of approval made the student feel confident.

Here, approval is about a person's judgment or reaction — not a legal or official act.

2. An Official Decision That Allows Something to Happen

This is the formal, authoritative sense. When a company, government, boss, bank, or any authority officially agrees to let something happen — after examining it — that is called an approval. In this sense, it is often the final step before something can start or be used.

Without this approval, the thing often cannot proceed. It is a kind of green light from someone in a position of power.

Examples:

  • The new medicine has not yet received government approval.
  • She submitted her project plan and is waiting for the manager's approval.
  • The loan approval came through, so they could buy the house.
  • Building a new bridge requires approval from several departments.

In everyday business, legal, and administrative life, this sense of approval is everywhere. It carries a sense of gatekeeping — the power to say "yes" officially.
Approval as a Feeling Someone Seeks from Others

One very common and psychologically important use of "approval" is when a person wants others to think well of them — to validate them, accept them, or consider them good enough. This is deeply human.

When someone is described as seeking approval, it means they care greatly about what others think of them and want to be liked, praised, or accepted.

Examples:

  • He always tried to dress well because he craved approval from his peers.
  • She found it hard to make decisions without her mother's approval.
  • As a child, all he wanted was his father's approval.

This usage often appears in discussions about psychology, self-confidence, and relationships. Needing too much approval from others is often seen as a sign of insecurity. Acting freely without needing others' approval is seen as a mark of self-confidence.

"Approval" can be used both ways, and the meaning shifts slightly.

Uncountable (no "a" or "an," no plural): This is the general feeling or act of approving. It refers to the concept or quality.

  • "She smiled in approval." (the feeling itself)
  • "The idea won widespread approval." (the general positive reception)

Countable (can say "an approval" or "approvals"): This refers to a specific, individual act of formally approving something.

  • "The project needs three separate approvals before it can begin."
  • "Each approval takes around two weeks to process."

These fixed phrases appear very often in English and are worth knowing:

Stamp of approval / Seal of approval:
When something receives the "stamp of approval," it means it has been officially accepted or endorsed — often by someone whose opinion matters. The phrase comes from the image of literally stamping a document to mark it as accepted.

  • "The recipe got the stamp of approval from the head chef."

Nod of approval:
A nod of approval is a gesture — a small, positive movement of the head — that shows you agree or are pleased. It is also used figuratively to mean any quiet, informal sign of acceptance.

  • "The director gave a nod of approval after watching the rehearsal."

On approval:
This is used in commerce. When goods are sent "on approval," the buyer receives them, examines them, and can return them if they are not satisfied — paying only if they decide to keep them.

  • "The antique dealer sent the vase on approval so the client could decide."

Win someone's approval / Gain approval:
To succeed in making someone accept or be pleased by something.

  • "It took months to win the board's approval for the new plan."

Withhold approval / Deny approval:
To refuse to give the formal go-ahead.

  • "The bank withheld approval because the applicant's income was too low."

Seek approval:
To actively try to get someone's agreement, permission, or positive judgment.

  • "She sought approval from the committee before launching the campaign."

Not all approval is the same. Here are some varieties you'll encounter:

  • Enthusiastic approval — strong, excited agreement ("The crowd greeted the announcement with enthusiastic approval.")
  • Tacit approval — approval that is not stated openly but is understood from someone's silence or inaction. If you don't object, it may look like you approve.
  • Reluctant approval — when someone agrees, but unwillingly ("He gave his reluctant approval to the plan.")
  • Conditional approval — approval that comes with strings attached ("The loan received conditional approval — they would lend the money only if she provided a guarantor.")
How "Approval" Is Different from Similar Words

Several words are close in meaning but not identical. Understanding the differences will sharpen your grasp of "approval."

Approval vs. Permission:
Permission is specifically about allowing someone to do something. Approval is broader — it can be about judging the quality of something, expressing satisfaction, or granting authorization. Every permission involves a kind of approval, but not every approval is a permission.

  • "She gave her permission for him to leave early." (he asked to leave; she allowed it)
  • "She expressed her approval of his decision." (she judged it and found it good — no action was necessarily being allowed here)

Approval vs. Consent:
Consent is specifically about agreeing to something that will happen to you, or that affects you personally. It carries a strong sense of personal agreement and is especially used in legal, medical, and ethical contexts. Approval is more general and can apply to third-party situations too.

  • "The patient gave consent for the surgery." (it's happening to them)
  • "The committee gave approval for the project." (they are evaluating something, not necessarily something that affects them directly)

Approval vs. Endorsement:
An endorsement is a public, often enthusiastic declaration of support — usually from someone well-known or respected. Approval is quieter and more general. An endorsement is a strong, public form of approval.

  • "The celebrity's endorsement of the product boosted its sales."
  • "The teacher's approval meant a lot to the student."

Approval vs. Acceptance:
Acceptance means something has been received or taken in — it is more passive. Approval involves making a positive judgment. You can accept something without fully approving of it.

  • "She accepted his apology." (she received it, moved on)
  • "She approved of the way he had handled the situation." (she judged it and found it good)
A Summary to Tie It All Together

Approval is the noun that captures the idea of judging something and finding it to be good, acceptable, or satisfactory — or of officially authorizing something. It lives in two worlds at once: the personal world of feelings and reactions, and the formal world of institutions, decisions, and power.

When a parent looks proudly at their child, when a government clears a drug for use, when a boss signs off on a budget, when an audience erupts in cheers — all of these involve approval in some form. What they share is this: something was looked at, judged, and found to be good enough to receive a "yes."
948:
To approve means to say "yes" to something — either officially, or in your own mind and heart.

That single idea — saying yes — plays out in two distinct ways, and understanding both is the key to truly knowing this word.
Meaning 1: To Officially Accept, Permit, or Authorize

This is the more formal and action-oriented sense. When a person or organization approves something, they look at it, evaluate it, and then give it the green light — making it official, valid, or allowed to move forward.

Think of it like a stamp of authority. The approval makes something legitimate.

Examples:

  • The manager approved the budget. (She said yes to the budget plan — now it's official.)
  • The bank approved his loan application. (They accepted it and will give him the money.)
  • The government approved a new law. (They passed it; it is now in force.)
  • The doctor approved the medication for patients over 60. (Cleared it for use in that group.)
  • My leave request was approved. (My boss said yes, and it's now officially allowed.)

In this sense, approving something has real-world consequences — money gets released, projects begin, laws take effect, or plans proceed. Without the approval, things cannot move forward.

Who can "approve" in this sense?
Usually someone in a position of authority — a manager, government body, committee, judge, bank, regulator, or institution. But it doesn't have to be powerful figures; even a teacher approving a topic for a student's essay counts.
Meaning 2: To Think Positively of Something or Someone

This is the more personal, internal sense. When you approve of something or someone, you feel that it is good, right, acceptable, or satisfactory — based on your values, standards, or judgement. No official action is taken; it is purely about your attitude or opinion.

Notice the key grammatical difference here: this meaning almost always uses "approve of" (with the word of), not just "approve."

Examples:

  • Her parents approve of her boyfriend. (They think he is a good person; they are happy with the relationship.)
  • I don't approve of lying, even for small reasons. (I think it is wrong; I have a negative opinion of it.)
  • He approves of the way she handled the situation. (He thinks she did the right thing.)
  • She doesn't approve of children using mobile phones too much. (She believes it is not good for them.)

Here, approving something doesn't change any official outcome. It simply tells us what someone thinks or feels about it. This sense is closely linked to personal values, morals, and beliefs.
The Critical Grammatical Point: "Approve" vs. "Approve of"

This is important and often confuses learners.

  • Approve + something (no "of") → formal, official authorization
    • The committee approved the proposal. ✅
  • Approve of + something (with "of") → personal opinion or attitude
    • The committee approved of the proposal. ✅ (They liked it / thought it was good)
    • She approved of his decision. ✅ (She thought it was a good decision)

Both are correct, but the meaning shifts. When you drop of, the word leans official. When you add of, it becomes about judgment and attitude.

However, in everyday English, the line can blur, especially in formal settings where an organization both officially accepts and holds a positive view of something at the same time.

Approval is not always full or enthusiastic. Someone can:

  • Fully approve — completely support something
  • Grudgingly approve — say yes, but reluctantly
  • Conditionally approve — say yes only if certain conditions are met ("The plan was approved, provided the budget is reduced.")
  • Not approve / disapprove — say no or hold a negative view

The opposite of "approve" is disapprove (to reject or think negatively of something).

It's worth being clear about what approve does not mean:

  • It does not mean simply to like something casually (you wouldn't say "I approved of the ice cream flavour" in normal speech — that would sound oddly formal for a minor preference).
  • It does not mean to prove something. Despite looking similar, "approve" and "prove" are unrelated in meaning.
  • It does not mean to praise someone — approval is about acceptance or a positive judgment, not necessarily complimenting someone out loud.

Since you will encounter this word family often, here they are:

  • Approved (adjective) → an approved method, government-approved
  • Approving (adjective) → an approving nod, she gave him an approving look (meaning she looked at him with satisfaction or agreement)
  • Approvingly (adverb) → He smiled approvingly. (He smiled in a way that showed approval)
  • Approval (noun) → She received approval for her plan. / He seeks his father's approval.
  • Disapprove (opposite verb) → I disapprove of that behavior.
  • Unapproved (adjective) → an unapproved drug, unapproved expenses
Common Collocations (Words That Go Naturally With "Approve")

In formal/institutional contexts:

  • Approve a plan / proposal / budget / project / bill / law / drug / design / application / request

In personal/opinion contexts:

  • Approve of a decision / choice / behavior / lifestyle / method / person

With adverbs:

  • Formally approve, officially approve, unanimously approve (everyone agreed), conditionally approve, tentatively approve (for now, but not finalized)
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

SenseWhat it meansExample
OfficialTo authorize or formally acceptThe board approved the merger.
PersonalTo think well of; to regard as good or rightShe approves of hard work.

If you can remember these two strands — the official stamp and the personal thumbs-up — you have fully grasped this word in all its uses.
949:
To approve of something or someone means to think that it is good, right, or acceptable. It is your personal judgment — your inner feeling or opinion — that something meets a standard you believe in.

Think of it this way: when you approve of something, you are giving it a "thumbs up" in your mind. You are saying, "Yes, this is good. This is the right thing."

Examples:

  • I approve of your decision to study medicine. → I think your decision is a good one.
  • She doesn't approve of lying. → She thinks lying is wrong and unacceptable.
  • Do you approve of his behavior? → Do you think his behavior is correct?

"Approve of" is a phrasal verb — that means it is a verb ("approve") combined with a preposition ("of") to create a specific meaning. You must always keep "of" attached to it. You cannot say "I approve your decision" when you mean a personal opinion — you must say "I approve of your decision."

The word or idea that follows "of" can be:

1. A noun or pronoun

  • I approve of this plan.
  • She approves of him.

2. A gerund (verb + -ing)
This is very important. When you want to put another verb after "approve of," you must use the -ing form.

  • They don't approve of smoking indoors.
  • He approves of working from home.
  • My parents don't approve of staying out late.

You would never say: They don't approve of to smoke. Always use the -ing form.

These two look similar but have different meanings, and mixing them up is a very common mistake.

"Approve" (without "of") is a formal or official word. It means to officially authorize or formally accept something, usually in a professional or institutional setting.

  • The government approved the new law. → They formally passed it into law.
  • The manager approved the report. → He gave his official sign-off.

"Approve of" (with "of") is about a personal opinion or attitude — it lives in your mind and heart, not in a document.

  • I approve of the new law. → I personally think it is a good law.
  • The manager approves of how the team works. → He has a positive personal opinion of it.

So: "Approve" = official action. "Approve of" = personal feeling/judgment.

People sometimes wonder: isn't "approve of" just a fancy way of saying "like"? Not exactly. There is a meaningful difference.

"Like" is about personal pleasure or enjoyment. It is emotional and subjective.

  • I like chocolate ice cream. → It pleases me. I enjoy it.

"Approve of" is about judgment — thinking something is right, correct, or morally acceptable. It is more rational and evaluative.

  • I approve of eating healthy food. → I think it is the right thing to do.

The difference becomes very clear in a sentence like this:
"I don't like vegetables, but I approve of my children eating them."

This makes perfect sense. You don't enjoy vegetables yourself (no "like"), but you still think it is the right and good thing for your children (approval). If "like" and "approve of" meant the same thing, this sentence would be a contradiction. They do not.
The Feeling of Authority in "Approve of"

"Approve of" often carries a subtle sense that the speaker feels they have the standing or right to judge. This is why it is so commonly used by:

  • Parents talking about their children's choices
  • Elders talking about younger people's behavior
  • Society judging norms and actions

Her parents don't approve of her boyfriend. — The parents feel they have a say in the matter.
I don't think our neighbors approve of loud music. — The neighbors have a view they stand by.

This doesn't always mean the speaker actually has authority, just that they are expressing their evaluative opinion. Anyone can approve or disapprove of anything.

This is actually one of the most common ways this phrase is used in real life. Disapproval comes up often in conversation.

  • I don't approve of cheating. → I think cheating is wrong.
  • She doesn't approve of the way he talks to people. → She thinks it is unacceptable.
  • Many people didn't approve of the new policy. → Many people thought the policy was bad.

You can also say "cannot approve of" to make the disapproval feel stronger or more principled:

  • I cannot approve of this kind of treatment. → I find it completely unacceptable.

Approval is not always black and white. You can modify "approve of" to show how strongly you feel:

  • I fully approve of this. → 100% positive opinion.
  • I strongly approve of what she did. → Very positive opinion.
  • I somewhat approve of the plan. → Partially positive, not entirely.
  • I don't entirely approve of it. → There are parts I have doubts about.
  • I don't approve of it at all. → Complete disapproval.

Sometimes, what is being approved of is already understood from the conversation, and the speaker drops the object entirely:

  • "I want to quit my job." — "I approve." (= I approve of that decision.)
  • "My parents don't approve." (= They don't approve of what I'm doing / who I'm with.)

This shorter form sounds natural in speech and informal writing.
Common Collocations (Words Often Seen with "Approve of")

Here are real patterns you will frequently see:

  • approve of someone's decision/choice/behavior/lifestyle
  • approve of the idea/plan/proposal
  • approve of the way someone does something
  • don't approve of violence/lying/cheating
  • fully / strongly / wholeheartedly approve of
  • not entirely / not really approve of

ConceptExplanation

"Approve of" means to hold a personal opinion that something or someone is good, right, or acceptable. It is always followed by a noun, pronoun, or a verb in the -ing form. It differs from plain "approve," which is about official authorization. It differs from "like," which is about personal pleasure. It often carries a sense of judgment or evaluation, and it is just as commonly seen in the negative ("don't approve of") as in the positive. The strength of approval can be increased or reduced with adverbs like "fully," "strongly," or "not entirely."

If you can remember one sentence, remember this one, because it captures the heart of the phrase:
"My parents approve of my career choice" — they think it is good and right, they give it their mental blessing.
950:
When something is approximate, it is close to the real or exact value, but not perfectly precise. It is a "nearly right" answer — good enough to be useful, but not 100% accurate.

Think of it like throwing a dart at a bullseye. An approximate answer hits near the center — not the outermost ring, and not the exact bullseye either. It lands in that honest, useful middle zone.

The key idea inside "approximate" is controlled closeness. It does not mean a wild guess, and it does not mean perfection. It sits deliberately between those two extremes.

When you say something is approximate, you are communicating two things at once:

  • "This is close to the truth."
  • "This may not be the exact truth."

Both of those ideas live inside the word simultaneously. That is what makes it precise and honest as a word — it signals confidence and a small admission of uncertainty at the same time.

Time: If someone asks what time it is and you say "it's about 3 o'clock," that's an approximate time. The real time might be 2:58 or 3:04, but "about 3" is close enough to be useful.

Distance: "The station is approximately 2 miles away." It might be 1.8 miles or 2.2 miles — but saying "about 2 miles" gives the other person a truthful, usable answer.

Age: "She is approximately 40 years old." You're not sure if she is 38 or 42, but she clearly isn't 25 or 60.

Money: "The repairs will cost approximately $500." The final bill might be $480 or $530, but you're telling someone the honest ballpark.

In every case, "approximate" signals: "I'm giving you a real, reasonable figure — not a made-up number, but also not a guaranteed exact one."
The Spectrum: From Rough to Exact

It helps to see "approximate" on a scale:

Wild guess → Rough estimate → Approximate → Close approximation → Exact

"Approximate" lives on the right side of this scale — meaning it leans toward accuracy. It is not a rough or careless figure. An approximate value has been thought about and is genuinely near the truth. The gap between an approximate value and the exact value is small and reasonable, not large and sloppy.

This is an important distinction: approximate is not an excuse for being lazy or wrong. It is an honest acknowledgment that you are very close, but not claiming a precision you don't have.
The Level of "Closeness" Depends on Context

How close is "approximate" exactly? That depends on what you are measuring.

In everyday conversation, saying the drive takes "approximately 30 minutes" when it actually takes 27 minutes is perfectly fine — a 3-minute gap is close enough.

But in science or engineering, "approximate" might mean accurate to within 1% or 0.01% — because the context demands tighter closeness.

The word doesn't define a fixed gap. It simply promises that the gap between the stated value and the real value is small and acceptable for the situation.

• It is not a synonym for "wrong." An approximate value is still largely correct.
  • It is not the same as a "rough guess." A rough guess can be quite far off. Approximate implies genuine closeness.
  • It is not the same as "exact" or "precise." Those words claim zero error. Approximate honestly admits a small one.
  • It is not vague. Saying something is approximate is actually a specific and honest claim — it tells you exactly what kind of answer you're getting.
Why This Word Exists (and Why It Matters)

In real life, we rarely know things with absolute perfection. We don't know exactly how many people live in a city (people move every day). We don't know a recipe needs exactly 2.000 cups of flour. We don't know traffic will take precisely 18 minutes.

The word "approximate" exists because life is full of situations where being very close to the truth is genuinely valuable and honest — and pretending to know the exact answer would actually be less truthful.

Using "approximate" is a mark of intellectual honesty. It says: "I have given this real thought, I'm giving you a reliable number, and I'm being transparent that it may not be the exact figure."
Approximate (adjective): Nearly correct or exact — close enough to the truth to be genuinely useful, while honestly acknowledging it may not be perfectly precise.
951:
To approximate means to come close to something — without reaching it exactly.

When you approximate, you get near the target. Very near. Near enough to be meaningful and useful. But there is still a small gap between your approximation and the perfect match or exact value.

This idea of closeness without exactness is the soul of the word. Hold on to it, because every use of the verb traces back to it.

The verb "approximate" is used in two closely related ways:

Use 1 — To closely resemble or come near to something in nature, quality, or character

When one thing approximates another, it comes very close to being that thing — it behaves like it, looks like it, or functions like it — but is not exactly it.

Examples:

  • "The artificial sweetener approximates the taste of sugar."
    It tastes very much like sugar. Close enough that many people wouldn't notice the difference. But it is not sugar.
  • "This computer model approximates the behavior of a real human brain."
    The model works in ways that are strikingly similar to how a human brain works — but it isn't one.
  • "Her singing approximates the voice of the original artist."
    She sounds remarkably similar to the original — very close — but there's still a difference.
  • "These lab conditions approximate the climate of the deep ocean."
    The lab has been set up to be as close to deep-ocean conditions as possible, though not perfectly identical.

In each case, something is coming very close to something else — but the word honestly signals that a gap, however small, remains.

Use 2 — To estimate or calculate a value that is close to the real one

When you approximate a number, quantity, or measurement, you work out a figure that is near the true value — not exact, but close enough to be useful and meaningful.

Examples:

  • "The scientists approximated the age of the fossil at 65 million years."
    They calculated a close, reasoned figure — not the perfectly precise number, but a well-supported near one.
  • "Can you approximate how long this project will take?"
    Can you give me a figure that's close to the real answer, even if not exact?
  • "The engineer approximated the cost of the bridge at $20 million."
    She gave a close, reasoned estimate — not a wild guess, but a careful near-figure.
  • "We approximated the population of the city at 3 million."
    We calculated a figure we know is very close to the true count.

Both uses are really the same idea expressed in different contexts.

In Use 1, you're saying: "This thing comes close to being that thing."
In Use 2, you're saying: "This number comes close to the true value."

In both cases, there is a real target — and the approximation is something that gets very close to it, but doesn't land exactly on it. The word never hides this gap. That honesty is built into its meaning.

Understanding these distinctions will give you a genuinely sharp grasp of the word.

1. Approximating is not the same as guessing.

A guess is random — you pick something with no particular reason to believe it's close. An approximation is deliberate and reasoned. When you approximate, you use whatever information or reasoning you have to arrive at something as close as possible to the real value or the real thing. An approximation has a foundation. A guess may not.

  • "I guessed the number was 5,000" → picked without calculation.
  • "I approximated the number at 4,800" → arrived at through careful reasoning.

The verb "approximate" carries a quiet implication of skill or effort — you are doing something methodical to get close.

2. The word carries honest acknowledgment of imprecision.

When you say "I approximated the distance," you are openly stating that you are not being exact. You are telling your listener: "This is close, but not perfect." This is what makes the word valuable in scientific, technical, and precise writing — it lets you communicate a result while being transparent about its limitations.

This honesty is one of its most important qualities. The word doesn't pretend to be exact when it isn't.

3. Approximating is not the same as imitating or copying.

When something approximates something else, it naturally comes close to it — but this doesn't mean someone deliberately copied or imitated it.

  • "This natural process approximates what the machine does artificially."
    The process happens to be very similar. No copying is implied.

Compare this with "imitate," which strongly suggests deliberate copying. "Approximate" is more neutral — it simply describes closeness, whatever the reason for that closeness.

4. A good approximation is a close one.

The word carries an implied standard: you want your approximation to be as close as possible to the real thing or real value. An approximation that is very far off is a poor approximation. The closer it is, the better.

This means the word isn't an excuse for sloppiness — it's a precise claim that you have gotten close, while being honest that you haven't reached exactness.

5. The gap can be tiny or moderate — but it is always real.

Even if something "very closely approximates" another thing, the word always implies there is some difference. The moment something is perfectly identical, you would no longer say it "approximates" — you would say it is the thing, or matches it exactly. Approximation lives in the space between "a bit off" and "nearly perfect."
How It Differs from Similar Words

Approximate vs. estimate:
These overlap heavily in Use 2. "Estimate" is the more general, everyday word for forming a rough judgment about a quantity. "Approximate" is slightly more precise in tone — it emphasizes that the value you've arrived at is specifically close to the real one, often in a mathematical or technical sense. You can almost always use either, but "approximate" sounds more deliberate and measured.

Approximate vs. resemble:
"Resemble" means to look or seem like something. "Approximate" is stronger — it means to come very close to being something, not just to look a bit like it. Something that approximates another thing is much closer to it than something that merely resembles it.

Approximate vs. simulate:
To "simulate" means to deliberately recreate the conditions, behavior, or appearance of something — usually using technology or a controlled system. "Approximate" is looser — it doesn't require deliberate recreation. Something can approximate something else simply by naturally being very similar to it.

Approximate vs. approach:
To "approach" something means to come near to it, often in the sense of getting closer and closer over time. "Approximate" focuses more on how close you are, rather than the movement toward it. The two sometimes overlap, but "approximate" is more about a state of closeness, while "approach" is more about the direction of movement.

Here are the natural ways the verb is used in sentences:

  • Subject + approximates + object:
    "This simulation approximates reality."*
  • Subject + approximated + object + at + [value]:
    "The team approximated the total cost at $500,000."*
  • Subject + approximates + to + object (slightly formal, used in British English):
    "This solution approximates to what we were looking for."*
  • Passive voice:
    "The age of the artifact was approximated at 10,000 years."*
    "The solution can be approximated using these formulas."*
  • Preceded by adverbs of degree:
    "The painting closely approximates the style of the original."*
    "The result only roughly approximates the true value."*
    "The process loosely approximates what happens in nature."*

The word "closely" is the most common adverb to appear with it, because "closely approximates" neatly captures the sense of being very near but not exact.
When You Would Use This Verb

You would reach for "approximate" as a verb when:

  • You want to say that something comes very close to being something else, while honestly acknowledging it isn't exactly that thing.
    "The treatment approximates the body's natural immune response."
  • You want to give a rough but careful figure, making clear you aren't claiming exactness.
    "We can approximate the time needed at four hours."
  • You want to be precise about the fact that you are not being fully precise — especially in scientific, technical, or formal writing.
    "The model approximates the real-world conditions as closely as possible."
  • You want to describe how close two things are to each other, without saying they are identical.
    "No description can perfectly approximate the feeling of loss."

If you remember only one thing: to approximate is to come very close to something, without reaching it exactly — and to be honest about that gap.

Whether it's a number, a quality, a feeling, a process, or a value — "approximate" always lives in that honest space between "not quite" and "nearly there."
952:
An approximation is something — a number, a value, a description, or an answer — that is close to the real or exact thing, but not perfectly identical to it. It is near enough to be useful and meaningful, even though it falls short of being completely precise.

Think of it this way: if the true answer to something is 98.7, and you say "roughly 100," that 100 is your approximation. It is not the exact truth, but it is close enough to give you — and others — a clear, workable sense of reality.

The word carries two closely linked meanings depending on how it is used in a sentence, and understanding both will make you fully fluent with it.

Meaning 1 — A result or value that is nearly (but not exactly) correct.

This is the most common use. Here, an approximation is the thing itself — the number, the answer, or the description that stands in place of the exact truth.

"The population of the city is approximately 4 million" — here, 4 million is the approximation. The real number might be 3,947,200, but 4 million is close enough to communicate the idea clearly.

Meaning 2 — The act or process of getting close to something without reaching it exactly.

Sometimes the word refers to the action of approaching something closely, not just the result. It describes the idea of being in the neighborhood of the truth.

"By approximation, scientists calculated the distance to the star." — here, approximation describes the method used.

In everyday life, Meaning 1 is far more common. You will almost always encounter "approximation" as a thing — a close-but-not-exact value or description.
Why Approximations Exist — and Why They Matter

You might wonder: why not just use the exact answer every time?

The honest truth is that exact answers are often impossible, impractical, or unnecessary.

  • A doctor estimating a patient's age from an X-ray cannot be exact. An approximation of "35 to 40 years old" is the best available answer — and it is enormously useful.
  • The value of pi (π) is 3.14159265358979… and goes on forever without repeating. Engineers use 3.14159 as an approximation. It is not perfect, but it is accurate enough to build bridges, design machines, and land spacecraft.
  • When you say "the drive takes about 2 hours," you are giving an approximation. You do not know the exact time down to the second, and the other person does not need it. Close is enough.

This is the deep, important truth about the word: an approximation is not a failure to find the right answer. It is a deliberate, intelligent choice to use a close answer because it is good enough for the purpose at hand. Approximations are everywhere in science, mathematics, engineering, medicine, and everyday conversation — not because people are lazy, but because precision has limits and usefulness has priorities.

Not all approximations are equal. The word naturally comes in degrees, and the English language reflects this.

A rough approximation is one that is in the general ballpark but not very tight. It gives you a broad sense, not a fine one.

"There were roughly a thousand people at the concert" — this could mean anywhere from 700 to 1,300. It is a rough approximation.

A close approximation (also called a good approximation) is one that is very nearly exact — so near that, for most purposes, it behaves just like the real thing.

"22 divided by 7 is a close approximation of pi." — it equals 3.1428..., which is very near the true value of 3.14159...

A first approximation is a starting estimate that you know you will refine later. It is used in science and problem-solving to mean: "This is our best guess right now, which we will improve as we learn more."

"As a first approximation, let us assume the surface of the earth is perfectly smooth." — scientists say this knowing it is not true, but it simplifies the problem enough to get started.

The idea of a spectrum matters because when someone uses the word "approximation," it always implies a gap from the truth — but the size of that gap can vary enormously.

Understanding what the word does not mean is just as important as knowing what it does mean.

It is not a wild guess. A guess is random — you throw out a number with no basis. An approximation, by contrast, is grounded. It comes from real information, calculation, or reasoning. It is systematically close to the truth, not accidentally so. If you guess someone weighs "60 kilograms" with no information, that is a guess. If a doctor looks at a patient's build and says "approximately 80 kilograms," that is an approximation — rooted in observation and judgment.

It is not an error. An error is an unintentional mistake — something you got wrong when you were trying to get it right. An approximation is deliberate. You know it is not exactly right, and you are choosing to use it anyway because the context allows or demands it.

It is not an exact value. The moment a value is exact — perfectly true, with no rounding or estimation — it stops being an approximation and simply becomes the answer. An approximation always carries the quiet acknowledgment: "this is close, but not quite."

Seeing the word across many situations will make its meaning stick firmly.

In mathematics: "The fraction 3/8 is a reasonable approximation of the decimal 0.375." (In this case it happens to be exact — but in general, fractions are used as approximations of irrational or long decimal numbers.)

In science: "Newtonian mechanics is an excellent approximation of reality when objects are moving much slower than the speed of light." — meaning: Newton's laws are not perfectly true at all scales, but they are so close to true in everyday conditions that they work brilliantly.

In everyday life: "An hour is a fair approximation of how long the meeting lasted" — it might have been 53 minutes or 67 minutes, but "an hour" communicates it well enough.

In descriptions of similarity: "The color of the ocean that day was an approximation of the deepest blue you have ever seen." — here the word is used more poetically to say: it was close to, but not quite, the deepest blue. This use is slightly less common but perfectly valid.

These are the natural, idiomatic ways the word is used, which you will see and hear regularly:

  • "as an approximation" — meaning: taking this as a close-enough stand-in for the truth. "We can use 10 as an approximation here."
  • "a rough/close/good/fair approximation" — describing how tight or loose the approximation is.
  • "a first approximation" — an initial, improvable estimate.
  • "to a good approximation" — meaning: the statement that follows is very nearly true. "To a good approximation, the Earth orbits the sun in a circle." (It is actually an ellipse, but barely.)
  • "an approximation of [something]" — identifying what the approximation is trying to represent. "This sketch is only an approximation of what the building will look like."
The One-Sentence Definition You Can Always Rely On

If you ever need to recall the meaning quickly:

An approximation is a value, result, or description that is deliberately close to — but not exactly — the true or ideal thing, used when exactness is impossible, impractical, or unnecessary.

Every other meaning, nuance, and use of the word flows from this core. Hold onto that, and the word will never confuse you again.
953:
An appurtenance is something that belongs to or goes along with something more important — not as the main thing itself, but as a secondary thing that is naturally attached to it, associated with it, or considered part of it.

Think of it this way: the main thing is the star, and the appurtenance is its supporting cast. The appurtenance doesn't stand on its own — it exists in relation to something bigger and more central.

Imagine you buy a house. The house itself is the main thing. But along with the house comes a garden shed, a driveway, a mailbox, and maybe even a right to use a path through your neighbor's land. None of these things are the house, but they all belong to it and come with it. These extras — these attached, secondary things — are the appurtenances of the house.

The word carries the idea of belonging and attachment. An appurtenance isn't just any random extra. It specifically belongs to something and is subordinate to it. Remove the main thing, and the appurtenance loses its reason for being there.
Where You'll See It Most: Property Law

The word is most commonly and precisely used in legal language, especially in property and real estate law.

When a piece of land or a building is sold, legal documents often say it is being transferred "together with all its appurtenances." This phrase is doing important work — it means the buyer gets not just the land itself, but everything legally attached to it. This can include:

Physical things like outbuildings (a barn, garage, or shed built on the land), fences, and fixtures permanently attached to the property.

Legal rights attached to the land — and this is where it gets especially interesting. For example, if your land has a right-of-way (a legal right to cross a neighbor's property to reach a road), that right is an appurtenance to your land. It doesn't exist separately — it belongs to your land, and when your land is sold, that right transfers to the new owner automatically. The same goes for easements (the right to use part of another's property for a specific purpose, like running a pipeline through it).

In this legal sense, an appurtenance is something so closely connected to a property that it is considered part of it in the eyes of the law, even if it isn't physically the land or building itself. The test lawyers often use is this: does this thing serve the main property, and is it intended to go with the property when sold? If yes, it is likely an appurtenance.

Outside of law, the word is used more broadly and often with a slightly literary or formal flavor. Here, appurtenances (it often appears in the plural in this usage) simply means the accessories, trappings, or accompaniments that typically come with something — especially something of status, rank, or importance.

For example: "He had acquired all the appurtenances of wealth — a grand estate, fine horses, and an army of servants." The wealth is the central thing; the estate, horses, and servants are its appurtenances.

Or: "She took on the role of mayor along with all its appurtenances — the office, the ceremonial chains, and the endless public duties." The position of mayor is central; everything that comes packaged with that role is an appurtenance of it.

In this usage, the word often carries a subtle undertone of things that are expected to accompany something, as if they are the natural equipment or trappings of it. It can even carry a slightly ironic or critical edge — implying that someone is focused on the outward accessories of something rather than its substance.

You will very frequently see this word in its plural form, appurtenances, because in most real-life situations there is more than one attached accessory or right. When someone says "with all its appurtenances," they are sweeping in everything that belongs to and comes with the main thing — the whole collection of secondary attached items — in one go.

Appurtenance carries a sense of formal completeness. When it is used, it signals: "we are not just talking about the main thing — we are talking about the main thing plus everything that rightfully belongs to it." It is a word that closes gaps and prevents oversights. In legal writing especially, it ensures nothing that is attached to a property gets accidentally left out of a transfer.

In literary or general use, it gives writing a sense of gravity and richness — it suggests that something comes with a whole world of associated things and meanings, not just its bare physical form.

If someone says "the king's throne was sold along with all its appurtenances," you now know exactly what that means: the throne was sold, and so was everything that belonged to it and went along with it — the cushion, the platform it stood on, perhaps certain ceremonial rights associated with it — the whole package, not just the chair itself.

That is appurtenance in a nutshell: a secondary thing that legitimately and naturally belongs to a more important primary thing, and which travels with it, serves it, and is defined by its relationship to it.
954:
Apricity is the warmth of the sun that you feel on your skin during cold weather, especially in winter.

That's the whole definition — but let's unpack it fully so it truly sticks.

You know those winter days when it's cold and crisp outside, but the sun is shining? You step outside, and even though the air is biting and your breath makes little clouds — you can feel the sun on your face, your hands, or your shoulders. It's a gentle, almost surprising warmth. The air around you is cold, but the sun's rays are landing on your skin and warming it directly.

That warmth — that specific, pleasant solar warmth felt during cold weather — is apricity.

It is not:

  • The warmth of a fireplace
  • The warmth of your coat
  • The general temperature of a warm day

It is only and specifically the sun's warmth as experienced against the cold.

You might think, "Can't I just say 'the sun feels warm'?" You can. But apricity captures something more precise and more poetic than that phrase does. It names the contrast experience — the special quality of warmth that only feels the way it does because of the surrounding cold. The cold makes you notice it. The cold makes it matter. Apricity is warm against something.

Think of it like the word "petrichor" — the smell of rain on dry earth. You could describe that smell in ten words, or you could just say petrichor. Apricity works the same way. It gives a name to a feeling everyone has had but few people had a single word for.

1. It is a noun, not an action.
Apricity is the warmth itself — the thing you feel. It is not the act of sitting in the sun (that would be the verb form, to apricate). So you experience apricity; you feel apricity; you sit in apricity. You don't "do" apricity.

2. The cold is essential.
Apricity is defined by its wintry context. A hot summer sun warming your skin is not apricity. The word specifically belongs to cold days — it is the warmth that arrives as a surprise guest in winter, felt through the cold air, not instead of it.

3. It is a rare, archaic word.
Apricity is considered an obscure or "lost" word in English. You will almost never encounter it in everyday speech or modern writing. It appeared in an English dictionary as far back as the 1600s and then quietly faded from common use. Today, it lives mostly among word lovers, poets, and people who enjoy collecting beautiful, precise words. Knowing it does not mean you'll hear it often — it means you'll have a name ready for a feeling you've already experienced many times.
How to Use It in a Sentence

• "She sat on the bench, eyes closed, letting the apricity wash over her cold cheeks."
  • "Even in the dead of February, there was apricity enough in the afternoon sun to make the walk worthwhile."
  • "He had forgotten how good apricity felt until that first sunny day after a week of grey skies."
Apricity is the specific warmth of the sun felt on your skin during cold or winter weather — a rare English word for a feeling everyone knows but almost no one had a name for.
955:
When something is described as apropos, it means it is perfectly fitting and remarkably relevant to the situation, topic, or moment at hand.

Not just vaguely related. Not just acceptable. But particularly well-matched to what is being discussed or what is happening — so well-matched that it's worth pointing out.
The One Idea That Defines It

Think of apropos as meaning: the right thing, in the right place, at the right time.

When something is apropos, there's almost a "click" moment — a sense that what was said, done, or referenced connects to the current situation so perfectly that it stands out. Like finding the one exact puzzle piece that fits, not just a piece that fits roughly.

Example 1: Your friend is complaining about how exhausting city traffic has become. You then remember an article you read last week about how commute times have doubled in major cities over the past decade. You bring it up. That fact is apropos — it connects directly and meaningfully to exactly what is being discussed right now.

Example 2: A professor is teaching a lesson about the consequences of greed. A student raises her hand and shares a story about a business that collapsed because its founders kept demanding more and more from investors. The professor nods and says, "That is a very apropos example." He means: that story fits this topic with striking precision.

Example 3: A politician gives a speech about the dangers of dishonesty in leadership. That very evening, a scandal breaks out revealing that he had lied on his résumé. A journalist writes: "The timing of the scandal was strangely apropos." Here, apropos captures the eerie, almost ironic sense that the scandal fit the day's topic unnervingly well.

Example 4: You are at a wedding where the couple met while hiking. The officiant opens with a quote about journeys and adventure. Everyone feels it — it's apropos. It isn't just a nice quote; it connects directly and meaningfully to who these people are.
How to Use It in a Sentence

Apropos can sit before a noun or after a linking verb.

Before a noun: "She made an apropos observation."
After a verb: "Your comment was surprisingly apropos."
With an intensifier: "The choice of music was entirely apropos."

It can also stand alone as a short response when something said or done fits the moment well — though that leans more conversational.
The Crucial Distinction: Apropos vs. Appropriate

This is one of the most important things to understand about this word, because learners often blur the two.

Appropriate means something is suitable and acceptable in a general sense — it doesn't violate norms, it matches what is expected, it is proper for the context. You can call a formal suit appropriate at a job interview. It says: "This belongs here. It's fine. It doesn't break any rules."

Apropos goes further. It is not about social rules or etiquette. It is about direct relevance and striking fittingness to what is specifically happening or being discussed right now. It says: "This doesn't just belong here generally — it connects to this specific topic or moment in a noticeably perfect way."

A comment can be completely appropriate (polite, inoffensive, socially correct) and yet not apropos at all (it has nothing to do with what's being talked about). On the other hand, something apropos will feel fitting to the moment — it adds something by virtue of how well it connects.

So: appropriate is about social acceptability; apropos is about contextual relevance and fittingness.

One thing that sets apropos apart from a word like "relevant" is that apropos implies the fittingness is worth remarking on. Something relevant just relates to the topic. Something apropos fits so well that it deserves a nod — it's striking in how well it matches.

This is why the word often carries a subtly appreciative or even impressed tone. When you call something apropos, you are essentially saying: "The fit here is so good, it's remarkable."

It can also carry a slightly ironic or wry tone (as in the journalism example above), where the fitting of something feels almost too perfect — almost coincidental in how well it connects to the moment.

It does not mean good or nice on its own. A compliment isn't apropos just because it's kind — it must be directly relevant to the specific moment.

It does not mean appropriate in the sense of proper behavior or dress code. Wearing a suit to a wedding is appropriate; it is not, by itself, apropos.

It does not mean timely in a general sense. Something can arrive on time and still be completely unrelated to what's happening. Apropos requires both timing and direct connection to the situation or topic.

Whenever you want to check if "apropos" fits, ask yourself this:

"Does this thing — this comment, story, quote, choice, or event — connect to what is specifically being discussed or happening right now in a way that is noticeably fitting?"

If yes, it's apropos. If it just sort of fits in a general way without any striking relevance, it probably isn't the right word.

Apropos is a precise, slightly elevated adjective that points to something fitting a specific moment or topic remarkably well — not just acceptably, not just in a general sense, but with a kind of notable, striking relevance. It is about context and connection. It is the word you reach for when something fits so well that you want to acknowledge the fit itself.
956:
"Apropos" as an adverb means at exactly the right moment, in a way that fits perfectly with what is already happening or being discussed. It carries a sense of: "This is so relevant, so fitting, so timely — it couldn't have been said or happened at a better moment."

Think of it as the feeling you get when someone says exactly the right thing at exactly the right time, almost as if it was planned — even though it wasn't.
What It Really Does in a Sentence

When you use "apropos" as an adverb, you are signaling one of two closely related things:

1. Something happened or was said at a fittingly perfect moment.

This is when timing and relevance collide. The event or remark didn't just happen — it happened right when it mattered most, in a way that felt almost too perfect to be coincidence.

He had been explaining how quickly life can change, and apropos, his phone rang with the news that he had been promoted.

Here, "apropos" tells you: the phone call arrived at a moment that fit the conversation so perfectly, it almost seemed designed to prove his point.

2. You're about to introduce a remark that is directly connected to what was just said — like "speaking of which" or "on that note."

This is the more common, everyday use. You place "apropos" at the start of a sentence to signal: "What I'm about to say connects directly and relevantly to what we were just discussing."

We were talking about how nobody reads anymore. Apropos, did you know that library memberships have dropped by 40% in the last decade?

Here, "apropos" tells the listener: "This fact I'm about to share is directly relevant — it fits right in with our conversation."
The Critical Distinction: "Apropos" vs. "By the Way"

This is where many learners go wrong, so pay close attention.

People often confuse "apropos" with "by the way," but they are not the same.

"By the way" introduces something that can be completely unrelated to the current topic. It's a polite way of changing or shifting the subject.

We were talking about football. By the way, did you pick up the groceries?

That is totally fine — the groceries have nothing to do with football. "By the way" doesn't claim relevance. It just redirects.

"Apropos", on the other hand, carries a promise of relevance. When you say "apropos," you are claiming that what follows connects to what came before. If it doesn't connect, you're misusing the word.

We were talking about football. Apropos, did you see that the star player just retired?

That works, because the retirement is directly relevant to football — the subject at hand. You wouldn't say "Apropos, did you pick up the groceries?" unless somehow the groceries were connected to what you were just discussing.

Think of it this way: "By the way" opens a new door. "Apropos" walks deeper through the same door you're already in.

"Apropos" carries a subtle but important tone: a mild sense of "how fitting" or "what a coincidence." It gently highlights the satisfying, sometimes surprising way something connects or arrives at just the right moment. It's a refined, precise word — slightly more formal than "speaking of which" — and it adds a layer of elegance to your observation.

When something happens "apropos," it doesn't feel random. It feels placed. It feels right.

Since "apropos" is about relevance and fittingness, avoid using it when:

  • The thing you're introducing has no connection to what was just being discussed.
  • You simply want to say "incidentally" about something random. (Use "incidentally" or "by the way" in that case.)
  • You want to say something is appropriate in a general, casual sense. (Use "appropriate" or "fitting" instead.)

Wrong use:

We were discussing climate change. Apropos, I had pasta for dinner last night.

That makes no sense, because pasta has nothing to do with climate change. "Apropos" makes a false promise here.

Right use:

We were discussing climate change. Apropos, a new report was just released showing record-breaking temperatures this summer.

That fits — the report is directly relevant to the topic.

Every time you see or use "apropos" as an adverb, remember one guiding question: Does this fit? Is this relevant? Does this land at exactly the right moment?

If the answer is yes, "apropos" is your word. It tells your reader or listener: "Notice how perfectly this connects. Notice how fittingly this arrived."

It is a small word that does a precise and elegant job — quietly pointing at the satisfying moment when the right thing appears at exactly the right time, in exactly the right place in a conversation.
957: "Apt" has two distinct meanings as an adjective. Both are common, and you need to know both to fully understand the word.
Meaning 1 — Exactly right or perfectly fitting

This is the most common meaning. When something is apt, it means it fits the situation so well that you couldn't have chosen better. Think of it as a "perfect match" — like a key that fits a lock exactly, with no wiggling, no forcing, just a clean fit.

This meaning is mostly used for:

  • words, descriptions, and comparisons
  • remarks and responses
  • names and titles

Examples:

  • "That is an apt description of how anxiety feels."
    The description captures the feeling so precisely that it couldn't be put better.
  • "The teacher made an apt comparison between electricity and water flowing through pipes."
    The comparison fits so well that it instantly makes the concept clear.
  • "He gave an apt reply — short, direct, and exactly what the moment needed."

The feeling behind this meaning: When you call something apt, you're saying: "Yes. That's exactly it. Nothing more, nothing less." It implies a kind of quiet perfection — the right word in the right place.
Meaning 2 — Having a natural tendency to do something

Here, "apt" means someone tends to do something or is likely to do something — almost out of habit or natural inclination. It describes a pattern of behavior that you've noticed, or that is characteristic of a person.

The structure is almost always: apt to + verb

Examples:

  • "She is apt to forget her keys."
    She has a habit of forgetting her keys. It's a recurring tendency.
  • "Children are apt to imitate what they see on TV."
    It's in their nature; they naturally tend to do it.
  • "He's apt to get emotional when talking about his hometown."
    You can expect it from him — it's a pattern.

The feeling behind this meaning: It's not a guarantee that something will happen, but based on past behavior or natural inclination, there's a good reason to expect it. It's softer than saying "always does" but stronger than "might do."
A third, rarer meaning — Quick and intelligent in learning

You'll occasionally see "apt" used to describe a learner or student who picks up things quickly and easily. This usage is less common today and mostly appears in formal or old-fashioned writing.

  • "She was an apt pupil and mastered the technique within a week."
    She learned fast and well.
How to tell which meaning is being used

It's very easy once you know both:

  • If "apt" is followed by a noun — an apt description, an apt metaphor, an apt name — it almost always means "fitting/exactly right."
  • If "apt" is followed by "to + verb" — apt to forget, apt to complain, apt to exaggerate — it means "tends to / likely to."
Apt vs. similar words — the fine differences

Apt vs. appropriate:
Both mean "fitting," but they're used differently. Appropriate is a broader word about whether something is socially or contextually acceptable — "Is this appropriate to say at a funeral?" It's about correctness. Apt is sharper — it's about how perfectly something fits, especially a description or comparison. You wouldn't say "an appropriate metaphor" as naturally as "an apt metaphor."

Apt to vs. likely to:
Both suggest something will probably happen. But likely focuses purely on the probability — "It's likely to rain." Apt to carries the additional sense of personal habit or natural tendency — "He's apt to exaggerate" tells you something about his character, not just a probability.

Apt to vs. prone to:
This is a subtle but important difference. Prone to almost always carries a negative flavor — it suggests a weakness or a bad habit. "He is prone to panic." Apt to is neutral — it can apply to positive, negative, or neutral behaviors. "She is apt to surprise you" is neutral or even positive. So if you're describing a flaw, prone often sounds more natural; if you're just describing a tendency without judgment, apt works better.
The overall personality of the word

"Apt" is a precise and slightly formal word. You'll see it more in writing than in casual speech, though it's not stiff or cold. Using it signals that you've chosen your words carefully. When you call something "apt," you're giving it a quiet compliment — you're saying it does its job exactly as it should. That's why writers and speakers who care about precision love this word.

If you ever want to remember both meanings at once, think of it this way:

Something apt fits perfectly. Someone apt to do something fits a pattern.

Both meanings share the same core idea: a clean, natural match between a thing and what it's supposed to do.
958:
Aptitude means a natural ability to learn or do something well — an inborn quality that makes a person pick up a particular skill faster and more easily than most other people.

Think of it this way: Two students sit in the same music class, receive the same teacher, and practice for the same number of hours. But one of them just gets it — they tune into rhythm instinctively, their fingers find the right notes more naturally, and they progress much faster. That student has an aptitude for music.

Aptitude is not something you build from scratch through hard work alone. It is something you are born with, or that comes to you naturally. It is the hidden engine inside you that makes certain things click with less effort.
The Critical Distinction: Aptitude vs. Skill

This is one of the most important things to understand about this word.

  • A skill is what you can already do — it is the result of learning and practice.
